result.summary: Aeetes, enraged at Argus's tale, sets Jason the deadly task of yoking his fire-breathing bulls and sowing serpent's teeth. Jason accepts, the Argonauts debate, and Argus proposes seeking Medea's magic aid, which a omen of a dove supports. Medea, tormented by love and a bad dream, struggles with shame before speaking to her sister Chalciope.

scenes.title: Aeetes sets the deadly trial
scenes.summary: Aeetes threatens the strangers, then offers the fleece if Jason can yoke his bulls and sow and reap the teeth. Jason reluctantly agrees and they leave, Medea watching.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks death by the fire-breathing bulls and armed earthborn men, and the Argonauts risk the king's wrath.

scenes.title: Medea's love-cares
scenes.summary: Medea broods on Jason and weeps, praying that he may survive.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks betraying her father and her own peace of mind through love for a stranger.

scenes.title: Council of the Argonauts
scenes.summary: Argus suggests asking Medea's help. The heroes volunteer to face the trial, a dove-and-hawk omen is read by Mopsus, and Idas scoffs. Argus is sent back to the city.
scenes.stakes: The crew risk death in the contest; Jason needs a way to win the fleece.

scenes.title: Aeetes plots in assembly
scenes.summary: Aeetes assembles the Colchians, threatens to burn the ship, and voices fear of a prophecy of betrayal by his offspring. Argus urges Chalciope to seek Medea's aid.
scenes.stakes: Aeetes fears losing his throne; the Argonauts risk destruction.

scenes.title: Medea's dream and hesitation
scenes.summary: Medea dreams she chooses the stranger over her parents, wakes in fear, and struggles with shame before approaching Chalciope. She speaks guilefully of her fears for the sons.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks family loyalty and her reputation against her growing love.

notable_quotes.reason: Jason's bitter line on dire necessity driving him.
Vivid picture of Medea's shame wrestling with desire.

analysis.text: Love is shown as an irresistible force pitted against shame and filial duty, setting up Medea's choice.
Hellenistic poetry like Apollonius's focuses on inner psychology, especially of women in love, departing from older epic.

legacy.text: Medea's hesitation before speaking to her sister influenced Roman poets, notably Virgil's portrayal of Dido in the Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: The dove-and-hawk omen is an Apollonian invention linking Aphrodite's bird to the aid Phineus promised.

language_notes.text: Aeetes means no one should ever again come seeking a fleece and a Phrixus; 'to his sorrow' is a threat that such a seeker will suffer.
Guest-friendship protects them: because they have eaten at his table, he cannot mutilate them. The 'feet alone' threat is a grim, ironic sparing.
Aeacus' son is Telamon, an Argonaut; Aeson's son is Jason. Patronymics replace names throughout.
The Sauromatae were a people of the lands north and east of the Black Sea, a plausible enemy for Aeetes.
'Plough-gates' are plough-lengths or acres, a measure of land; 'share' is the ploughshare, the blade that cuts the furrow.
The 'corn of Demeter' means grain; Demeter was goddess of agriculture. Sowing serpent's teeth recalls the myth of Cadmus, whose teeth grew into armed men.
'Holding her bright veil aside' shows Medea secretly watching; she is the maiden, though unnamed here.
"The Loves" are the Erotes, divine spirits of desire; Medea's brooding is shown as their work, after Eros's arrow struck her earlier in the book.
The "revered goddess, daughter of Perses" is Hecate, whom Medea serves as priestess and invokes here.
"Plough-gates" means a measure of ploughed land; the word is an old rendering of a Greek unit of area, roughly four acres' worth of work.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe" or "I think".
"Stern-ornament" is the curved decorative post at the ship's back end, the aphlaston.
Phineus, the blind prophet the Argonauts met earlier, told them their return depended on the Cyprian goddess, Aphrodite.
Enyalius is a title of Ares, the war god. Cypris is Aphrodite, named for Cyprus, where she was worshipped.
The Minyae are the Argonauts, named for the descendants of Minyas, an early Greek people from whom many of the heroes claimed descent.
Phrixus fled to Colchis on the golden ram sent by the gods and was received by Aeetes; Hermes is said to have guided the hospitality.
"Scatheless" means unharmed; "steadings" are farmsteads; "forays" are raids.
Helios, the Sun god, is Aeetes' father. The prophecy that his own offspring would betray him drives his suspicion of Medea and Apsyrtus' family.
"Achaean land" means Greece; Aeetes sarcastically claims he is sending Phrixus' sons home, as their father wished, on a long journey.
"Haply either fate should withstand" means she fears that fate might oppose her, so that her plea to Medea would fail.
The thrice-repeated attempt, with the fourth failing, is a folk-tale pattern showing Medea's mounting struggle.
"The bold Loves" refers to the Erotes, divine forces of desire, who here drive Medea beyond her modesty.

context_notes.text: Argus, son of Phrixus and Chalciope, has told Aeetes that the Argonauts came for the golden fleece, which Phrixus had left in Colchis.
Ares was the god of war. The bulls and the field are sacred to him, and the fleece hangs in his grove.
Argus is Aeetes' grandson and Jason's guide, so he alone stays with the Argonauts while his brothers wait.
Hecate was a goddess of witchcraft, night and crossroads. Medea is her priestess in Colchis.
Peleus (son of Aeacus), Telamon, Idas, Castor and Pollux (sons of Tyndareus) and Meleager (Oeneus' son) are among the greatest Argonauts.
Doves were sacred to Aphrodite, so the dove's escape signals her favour. The hawk is a natural enemy of doves.
Aeetes is king of Colchis, owner of the Golden Fleece, father of Medea, Apsyrtus and Chalciope.
Chalciope, Medea's elder sister, is the mother of Argus and his brothers, sons of Phrixus, who have allied themselves with the Argonauts.
Aeetes had set Jason the task of yoking fire-breathing oxen as the price of the fleece, and Medea's dream reflects her secret love for Jason.

literary_notes.text: The narrator frames Aeetes' rage in epic formula, heightening his danger before the speech.
Aeetes' divided purpose shows him as cunning as well as violent, weighing murder against a lethal test.
Jason's downcast eyes and silence show his helplessness, contrasting with the heroic image of an epic leader.
Medea's soul 'creeping like a dream' follows Jason, conveying her secret, helpless love and foreshadowing her aid.
Medea's mind replays his looks, clothes and words in vivid detail, showing how deeply love has gripped her.
She mourns Jason as if already dead, showing how quickly and fully her feelings have grown.
Medea turns to address Hecate directly, making her prayer and divided feelings feel immediate.
The dove falling into Jason's lap and the hawk's death stand for Aphrodite's protection of the hero and the failure of force.
Idas's scorn for women and for Cypris shows his boastful, arrogant nature and his contempt for the gods' ways.
The dream reveals Medea's hidden desires and the conflict between family loyalty and love for the stranger, foreshadowing her actual choice.
The repeated going and returning enacts Medea's inner conflict between shame and desire.
Medea's hesitation is compared to a silent, shamed young widow, conveying private grief and fear of mockery.
The word is imagined as a fluttering creature, showing Medea's struggle to speak.
Medea calls her dream ghastly for the sons' sake, but readers know it concerns her love for Jason.
